cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: What does the Roman law of things (property law) deal with?
cards.back:
It attributes legal objects (things, RES) to legal subjects, ie it governs property rights.
• Legal subject = anyone capable of rights and duties (legal personality).
• Things are the objects of legal transactions.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Which factors determined a person's legal status in Roman law?
cards.back:
An interplay of liberty, citizenship, position in the family and gender.
• STATUS LIBERTATIS: free (INGENUI, LIBERTI) vs slaves (SERVI).
• STATUS CIVITATIS: eg DOMINIUM EX IURE QUIRITIUM and MANCIPATIO only for citizens.
• STATUS FAMILIAE: SUI IURIS vs persons in PATRIA POTESTAS.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Can slaves and persons in PATRIA POTESTAS hold property?
cards.back:
No, neither can hold property in their own right; both can acquire for their DOMINUS / PATER FAMILIAS.
• Slaves are things: they can be sold or pledged.
• Children of the house and UXOR IN MANU are free (STATUS LIBERTATIS).

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: What does NASCITURUS PRO IAM NATO HABETUR, QUOTIENS DE COMMODIS EIUS AGITUR mean?
cards.back:
An unborn child is treated as already born whenever this is to its advantage.
• Otherwise legal personality begins at live birth (Paulus D 1.5.7).
• Consequence: a child born after the father's death may inherit.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: How does Roman law treat corporations (UNIVERSITATES), and what does Ulpian D 3.4.7.1 say?
cards.back:
Corporations are independent legal entities: they hold rights and act through representatives.
• SI QUID UNIVERSITATI DEBETUR, SINGULIS NON DEBENTUR.
• What the corporation owes or is owed is not its members'.
• Examples: RES PUBLICA, MUNICIPIA, COLLEGIA, SOCIETATES PUBLICANORUM.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Legal personality vs legal capacity — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Personality = capacity for rights and duties; capacity = ability to change them through one's own acts.
• Personality begins at birth (for the freeborn).
• Capacity requires maturity in age and mind.
• Capacity = capacity to act + criminal capacity.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Which age thresholds matter for capacity in Roman law?
cards.back:
INFANTES (under 7) lack capacity, PUPILLI have limited capacity, PUBERTAS brings full capacity.
• PUPILLI: boys 7–14, girls 7–12; need AUCTORITAS TUTORIS to incur obligations.
• PUBERTAS: girls at 12, boys at 14.
• Minors under 25 protected by LEX (P)LAETORIA and RESTITUTIO IN INTEGRUM.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: What is a NEGOTIUM CLAUDICANS?
cards.back:
A 'limping transaction': a PUPILLUS contracts without his tutor; only the part favourable to him binds.
• The other party is bound, the PUPILLUS is not (Ulpian D 19.1.13.29).
• A PUPILLUS may improve, but not worsen, his position alone.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Which groups besides minors had restricted capacity in Roman law?
cards.back:
Women SUI IURIS, mentally disabled persons (FURIOSI) and declared spendthrifts (PRODIGI).
• Women needed a TUTOR MULIERIS for formal acts; a formality by classical times.
• FURIOSI: no capacity; a CURATOR FURIOSI acts for them.
• PRODIGUS: declared incapable by the praetor (INTERDICTIO).

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: What are the typical features of property rights (rights IN REM)?
cards.back:
They give power over a specific thing, enforceable against everyone.
• Only over corporeal things, RES CORPORALES: QUI TANGI POSSUNT (that can be touched).
• Absolute: enforced against the world at large by ACTIONES IN REM.
• Relational rights (creditor–debtor) are enforced by ACTIONES IN PERSONAM.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — Basics: persons, things, property rights
cards.front: Which property rights does Roman law recognise, and what is the numerus clausus?
cards.back:
A closed list of rights in rem that parties cannot extend: the numerus clausus.
• DOMINIUM (REI VINDICATIO); SERVITUTES (VINDICATIO SERVITUTIS); PIGNUS (VINDICATIO PIGNORIS).
• EMPHYTEUSIS (REI VINDICATIO UTILIS); SUPERFICIES (ACTIO DE SUPERFICIE).
• Each type is protected by its own ACTIO IN REM.

cards.front: What is possession (POSSESSIO)?
cards.back:
Factual control over a thing coupled with the intention to control it.
• A fact, not a right: it shows who actually controls the thing.
• Protected only temporarily, by possessory interdicts.

cards.front: Possession vs ownership — what is the difference?
cards.back:
The possessor has the thing in his power (fact); the owner is entitled to have it (right).
• Possession says nothing about a right to the thing.
• Hector the thief acquires possession, but never ownership.

cards.front: Why is possession legally significant (II.B)?
cards.back:
It prevents conflict: the possessor is stronger in disputes, and possession founds acquisition of ownership.
• Possessor hands over only once the claimant proves his right.
• Ownership via TRADITIO, OCCUPATIO (ownerless things) or USUCAPIO.

cards.front: What are the two elements of possession?
cards.back:
ANIMUS (intent to possess, ANIMUS POSSIDENDI) and CORPUS (control over the thing).
• Both must be present for possession of a corporeal thing.
• Correct Latin: possession is acquired/retained ANIMO ET CORPORE.
• Sources say CORPORE POSSIDERE, never CORPUS alone.

cards.front: Does CORPUS require physical contact with the thing?
cards.back:
No: the thing must be within one's sphere of influence, so control can be exercised at will.
• Rusticus possesses his clothes and the cattle on his meadow.
• Paulus D 41.2.1.21: OCULIS ET AFFECTU suffices, not only CORPORE ET TACTU.
• But CORPUS is never purely symbolic.

cards.front: What is proprietary possession, and what is ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI?
cards.back:
Possession with the intention of having the thing for oneself (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI).
• Sources saying POSSESSIO usually mean proprietary possession.
• Can be exercised through another (mediate), eg lessee Lea for Rusticus.

cards.front: What is NATURALIS POSSESSIO (detention), and who are typical detentors?
cards.back:
Holding a thing for another (ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI) by a holder SUI IURIS; not proprietary possession.
• Typical detentors: tenants, leaseholders, lessees, depositaries, precarists.
• Jurists also use TENERE or HABERE.

cards.front: Detentor vs possessor's agent — what is the difference?
cards.back:
A detentor is SUI IURIS; a possessor's agent is ALIENI IURIS, the DOMINUS' 'extended arm'.
• Via a detentor the POSSESSOR has only mediate possession.
• Via an agent (slave Achilles taking sheep to market) possession is immediate.

cards.front: Immediate vs mediate possession — when does each arise?
cards.back:
Immediate: control personally or through persons in one's power; mediate: control through a detentor SUI IURIS.
• Clara deposits her vase with Midas: Clara mediate proprietary, Midas immediate natural possessor.
• Hector's theft ends both; Hector becomes POSSESSOR.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: IUSTA POSSESSIO vs POSSESSIO EX IUSTA CAUSA — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Both strengthen the possessor: IUSTA POSSESSIO is unflawed (interdicts); POSSESSIO EX IUSTA CAUSA rests on valid title.
• IUSTA = NEC VI NEC CLAM NEC PRECARIO, judged relationally.
• EX IUSTA CAUSA = civil possession: leads to ownership or USUCAPIO.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: What does NEC VI NEC CLAM NEC PRECARIO mean?
cards.back:
IUSTA POSSESSIO: obtained neither by force, nor secretly, nor by revocable grant (PRECARIUM).
• Prerequisite for interdict protection: POSSESSIO AD INTERDICTA.
• PRECARIUM: gratuitous use revocable at will; factual, unlike COMMODATUM.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: What are possessory interdicts and what is their aim?
cards.back:
Praetorian decrees in individual cases that prevent dispossession and stop escalating conflict over things.
• Only temporary: the right itself needs a petitory ACTIO IN REM.
• Also for some natural possessors: emphyteutic lessees, precarists, pledgees, sequesters.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: What is the EXCEPTIO VITIOSAE POSSESSIONIS?
cards.back:
The part of the interdict formula that denies protection to the INIUSTUS POSSESSOR.
• Applies if he obtained the thing VI, CLAM or PRECARIO from the opponent.
• He must then suffer forcible recapture or restitution by that opponent.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: In what sense is possessory protection relational (ALTER AB ALTERO)?
cards.back:
IUSTA POSSESSIO is assessed only in relation to the opponent, never objectively.
• A thief robbed in turn is protected against the robber.
• Owner Clara has an interdict against thief Hector, not bona fide Leander.
• Against Leander Clara needs an ACTIO IN REM.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: Prohibitory vs restitutory interdicts — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Prohibitory interdicts forbid force against the IUSTUS POSSESSOR; restitutory ones order the thing restored.
• Prohibitory: VIM FIERI VETO ('I forbid the use of force').
• Restitutory: RESTITUAS ('you shall restitute').
• Both are barred by the EXCEPTIO VITIOSAE POSSESSIONIS.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: What does VIM VI REPELLERE LICET mean, and when does it apply?
cards.back:
It is permitted to repel force with force.
• Against someone possessing VI towards you, you may retake by force.
• Leo drives Thisbe off her farm: Thisbe may regain it by force.
• One of the few cases of permitted self-help.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — IUSTA POSSESSIO, civil possession, interdicts
cards.front: What is civil possession (POSSESSIO CIVILIS) and what are its advantages?
cards.back:
Possession based on a valid title (IUSTA CAUSA), eg sale, donation, loan, dowry: POSSESSIO EX IUSTA CAUSA.
• From an authorised alienor: the possessor becomes owner (TRADITIO).
• From an unauthorised one: ownership possible by USUCAPIO.
• Leander has civil possession; thief Hector never does.

cards.front: What is FURTUM?
cards.back:
Taking another's movable property with intent to enrich oneself.
• Broader than modern theft: includes embezzlement and theft by finding.
• Depositary Diogenes selling Iris' vase commits FURTUM.
• No theft of land; LEGES IULIAE ET PLAUTIAE bar USUCAPIO of land seized by force.

cards.front: What are the elements of FURTUM?
cards.back:
Larcenous intent (DOLUS) manifested in an external act of taking a movable thing.
• DOLUS MALUS: knowingly taking another's thing to enrich oneself.
• Mere intent is not enough, even for a depositary (D 41.2.3.18).
• The depositary commits FURTUM only once he hides the thing away.

cards.front: What is the thief's position as regards possession?
cards.back:
He is POSSESSOR: the taking fulfils ANIMUS and CORPUS; his possession is original.
• Not civil possession: no IUSTA CAUSA.
• Flawed towards the victim (eg CLAM).
• Never ownership; RES FURTIVAE cannot be usucapted (LEX ATINIA).

cards.front: ACTIO FURTI vs CONDICTIO FURTIVA — what is the difference?
cards.back:
ACTIO FURTI is a penal action; CONDICTIO FURTIVA is reipersecutory, recovering the thing or its value.
• Penalty paid to the victim: fourfold (FURTUM MANIFESTUM), twofold (NEC MANIFESTUM).
• CONDICTIO only against the thief, even if the thing has perished.
• The two may be cumulated.

cards.front: CONDICTIO FURTIVA vs REI VINDICATIO — when to use which?
cards.back:
Both are reipersecutory, so they cannot be cumulated; the owner must choose.
• CONDICTIO FURTIVA: only against the thief; works even if the thing is gone.
• REI VINDICATIO: against any possessor, but only while the thing exists.

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about possession and its protection — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Who has which kind of possession, and on what grounds?
• ANIMUS and CORPUS present? Proprietary or natural possession (detention)?
• Immediate or mediate; detentor or possessor's agent?
• IUSTA towards the opponent (NEC VI NEC CLAM NEC PRECARIO)? Civil (IUSTA CAUSA)?

cards.front: Why are requirements stricter for acquiring possession than for retaining it?
cards.back:
Acquisition may change established ownership, so it needs clear, predictable rules evident to all.
• CORPUS is always decisive for acquisition.
• Once established, possession is kept without constant proof, sometimes even SOLO ANIMO.

cards.front: Can possession be transferred by symbols or documents in Roman law?
cards.back:
No: real factual control is always required.
• No TRADITIO PER CARTAM (by documents) and no TRADITIO FICTA (fictive transfer).
• CORPUS may exist without contact, but is never purely symbolic.

cards.front: Who can acquire possession in his own right, and can a PUPILLUS do so alone (Paulus D 41.2.1.3)?
cards.back:
Only persons SUI IURIS with sufficient understanding; FURIOSI cannot.
• Ofilius and Nerva: a PUPILLUS can, because possession is factual.
• Paulus: yes, once he has reached INTELLECTUS (sufficient maturity).
• Persons in POTESTAS cannot acquire in their own right.

cards.front: Original vs derivative acquisition of possession — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Original: by one's own act without the previous possessor; derivative: transferred by the previous possessor.
• Original: OCCUPATIO of a RES NULLIUS; also the thief.
• Derivative: TRADITIO from transferor to transferee.
• Derivative acquisition demands less CORPUS than original.

cards.front: Contract vs conveyance — why does it matter for ANIMUS POSSIDENDI?
cards.back:
A contract creates the obligation to transfer; the conveyance (eg TRADITIO) transfers the right itself.
• EMPTIO VENDITIO alone gives neither possession nor ownership.
• Intent to buy ≠ ANIMUS POSSIDENDI (cart bought 1 March, delivered 15 March).
• ANIMUS may be explicit or inferred from conduct.

cards.front: Ulpianus D 18.6.1.2 (Case 11): a wine buyer seals a barrel in the seller's cellar — does he acquire possession?
cards.back:
Labeo and Ulpian: no, sealing only prevents substitution and shows no ANIMUS POSSIDENDI.
• Trebatius: yes, sealing expresses possessory intent.
• CORPUS is unproblematic: he even touches the barrel.
• Contrast D 18.6.15(14).1: marking planks does give possession.

cards.front: What is IUS CONTROVERSUM?
cards.back:
Opposing juristic opinions on the same case or issue, all integrated into the corpus of Roman law.
• Example: Trebatius vs Labeo/Ulpian on the sealed barrel.
• No controversy where different facts explain different solutions.

cards.front: Which factors determine how much CORPUS is required for acquiring possession?
cards.back:
Mode of acquisition, type and form of the thing, and the social environment.
• Derivative needs less than original; land is easier to control than movables.
• Small handy things are easier to control than bulky stores.
• High risk of third-party interference demands a manifest act.

cards.front: Paulus D 41.2.3.1 (Case 1): must the acquirer of land walk round its whole perimeter?
cards.back:
No, it suffices to set foot on the land with the intent to acquire it.
• Setting foot on it is the general rule for land.
• Borderline (Celsus D 41.2.18.2): land shown from the buyer's own neighbouring tower.

cards.front: What does QUODAMMODO MANU LONGA TRADITA ('as if delivered by a long hand') describe?
cards.back:
Transfers of possession without a physical act of taking: the possibility of control suffices.
• Iavolenus D 46.3.79: money laid down before the creditor's eyes.
• Celsus D 41.2.18.2: goods placed in the buyer's empty house.
• Not a clearly defined legal concept.

cards.front: Paulus D 41.2.1.21 (Case 4): what does acquiring possession OCULIS ET AFFECTU mean?
cards.back:
Agreeing on immediate transfer in the presence of the goods suffices; no touching (CORPORE ET TACTU) needed.
• Four cases: buyer's PROCURATOR, coins to a third party, very heavy object, cellar keys.
• Keys fit only if handed over at the cellar (cf Papinianus D 18.1.74).

cards.front: Gaius (Trebatius) D 41.1.5.1 (Case 8): a hunter wounds a wild animal so it can be caught — is he possessor?
cards.back:
Gaius: only once he captures it — QUIA MULTA ACCIDERE POSSUNT, UT EAM NON CAPIAMUS.
• Trebatius: yes, as long as he pursues it.
• Strict CORPUS because OCCUPATIO is an original mode.
• Proculus D 41.1.55 (trapped boar): possession once IN MEAM POTESTATEM PERVENIT.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: Why are TRADITIO BREVI MANU and CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM called modes SOLO ANIMO — and is that accurate?
cards.back:
Because consensus (ANIMUS) dominates; inaccurately, as CORPUS is never entirely disregarded.
• Both remain acquisition CORPORE ET ANIMO.
• They are tradition surrogates: change without visible handover.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: What is TRADITIO BREVI MANU (delivery 'by a short hand')?
cards.back:
A detentor becomes possessor by agreement: the possessor gives up his ANIMUS, the detentor holds for himself.
• CORPUS already exists through the detention.
• Gaius D 41.1.9.5: borrower/lessee/depositary buys the thing; no return and redelivery.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: What is CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM (possessory agreement)?
cards.back:
The acquirer gets possession by agreeing that the current possessor or detentor will henceforth hold for him.
• The acquirer gains mediate possession; the transferor becomes his detentor.
• Ulpian D 6.1.77: a woman donates land and leases it back.
• Mirror image of TRADITIO BREVI MANU.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: What does NEMO SIBI IPSE CAUSAM POSSESSIONIS MUTARE POTEST mean?
cards.back:
Nobody can change the title (CAUSA) of his possession of his own accord.
• Self-declared possessor (thief, detentor) lacks IUSTA CAUSA: no civil possession or USUCAPIO.
• Tradition surrogates do not violate it: both parties agree.
• Basis of § 319 ABGB.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: What does ANIMO NOSTRO, CORPORE ALIENO mean (Paulus D 41.2.3.12)?
cards.back:
The DOMINUS acquires possession with his own intent through the physical control of a person in his power.
• Persons ALIENI IURIS cannot acquire for themselves, only for the DOMINUS.
• Papinianus D 41.2.48: donated slave sent back with a IUSSUM to acquire the estate.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: How do the DOMINUS' CORPUS and ANIMUS arise when he acquires through a person in his power?
cards.back:
CORPUS: his POTESTAS plus the dependant's actual control; ANIMUS: a IUSSUM or a PECULIUM.
• IUSSUM = order for one particular transaction.
• Without IUSSUM or PECULIUM no acquisition, unless later approved (RATIHABITIO).
• To acquire through a slave, the DOMINUS must possess the slave.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: What is a PECULIUM and what does it mean for acquiring possession?
cards.back:
Assets a DOMINUS lets a dependant manage independently: a general, abstract expression of his possessory intent.
• Covers all the holder's transactions; he concretises it: ANIMO SERVORUM.
• The DOMINUS acquires without knowing each deal (Paulus D 41.2.1.5).
• Dependant's own ANIMUS irrelevant; INTELLECTUS POSSIDENDI suffices.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: Could persons SUI IURIS acquire possession for another in classical law (direct vs indirect agency)?
cards.back:
No, generally only indirect agency: the agent acquires first, then transfers to the principal.
• Direct agency: the transaction immediately affects the principal.
• Secunda buys for Primus, then hands over in a separate transaction.
• Transferring possession through a SUI IURIS agent was always possible.

cards.topic: 14.10. Possession — SOLO ANIMO modes and acquisition through others
cards.front: Which persons SUI IURIS could exceptionally acquire possession directly for another?
cards.back:
CURATOR, TUTOR and PROCURATOR; Justinian later opened direct agency generally.
• PROCURATOR: often a freedman bound to his master.
• Ulpian D 41.1.20.2: Titius accepts delivery for co-buyer Ego QUASI PROCURATOR.
• That is analogy: solving an unregulated case by similarity to recognised ones.

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about the acquisition of possession — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Did the acquirer have ANIMUS POSSIDENDI and CORPUS at the decisive moment?
• Original or derivative; contract or conveyance; capacity (PUPILLUS, FURIOSUS)?
• CORPUS factors: type of thing, OCULIS ET AFFECTU, keys, social environment?
• Tradition surrogate (BREVI MANU, CONSTITUTUM) or acquisition through others (IUSSUM, PECULIUM, agent)?

cards.front: What does retaining possession require, and when does possession end?
cards.back:
ANIMUS and CORPUS, judged more leniently; it ends when intent is given up or all control is lost.
• SOLO ANIMO retention possible for a SERVUS FUGITIVUS and for land.
• Ends voluntarily (TRADITIO, abandonment) or involuntarily.

cards.front: Does losing possession also mean losing ownership?
cards.back:
Usually not: possession and ownership are lost separately.
• Goods thrown overboard in an emergency: possession lost, ownership kept.
• A finder who keeps obviously lost property is a FUR.
• Exception: a wild animal regaining freedom ends ownership too.

cards.front: How is retention of possession assessed for movables vs immovables?
cards.back:
Movables: only with CUSTODIA (exception SERVUS FUGITIVUS); immovables: SOLO ANIMO retention possible in two cases.
• Land without detentors or possessor's agents.
• Land where a detentor or possessor's agent was appointed.
• No single formula: analyse the case types.

cards.front: What basic tendency does Roman law show in retaining possession?
cards.back:
It preserves existing possession and avoids hasty changes of control.
• Change recognised only if likely to be permanent (Iavolenus D 41.2.22).
• TRADITIO to an incapable acquirer: transferor keeps possession (Ulpian) or loses it (Celsus).
• PUPILLI/FURIOSI cannot give up possession ANIMO without tutor/curator.

cards.front: What is CUSTODIA in the context of retaining possession of movables?
cards.back:
Control such that one can at any time lay hands on the thing or bring it within reach.
• Mislaid within one's sphere: possession kept (Paulus D 41.2.3.13).
• Lost outside one's sphere: possession lost (Pomponius D 41.2.25 pr).
• Forgotten buried money: kept while nobody intervenes (Papinianus D 41.2.44 pr).

cards.front: Ulpianus D 41.2.13 pr (Case 47): stones sink in the Tiber in a shipwreck and are later recovered — possession and ownership?
cards.back:
Possession is lost, ownership is not: the owner lost all control over the stones.
• Illustrates CUSTODIA as the test for movables.
• Contrast the SERVUS FUGITIVUS, possessed SOLO ANIMO.

cards.front: Who possesses a SERVUS FUGITIVUS (fugitive slave), what he took with him and what he acquires in flight?
cards.back:
The master retains possession SOLO ANIMO until a third party takes the slave; the rest follows.
• Master keeps possessing (and usucapting) the slave; no CUSTODIA needed (Paulus D 41.2.1.14).
• Things taken along: master's, through his possessory agent.
• Acquisitions: master's, as if under a valid PECULIUM (fiction).

cards.front: Can possession of land be retained SOLO ANIMO — since when and for how long?
cards.back:
Yes: first only for seasonal pastures (SALTUS); Proculus extended it to all land.
• Only with a view to re-establishing CORPUS, not indefinitely.
• Probably lost when possessor or agents failed to return as planned.

cards.front: A occupies B's land without permission, intending to possess — does A immediately acquire possession?
cards.back:
No: A acquires only if B makes no attempt to regain control, or his attempt fails.
• If B regains control, B remained possessor throughout.
• After losing it: interdicts UTI POSSIDETIS, UNDE VI; ACTIO PUBLICIANA, REI VINDICATIO.
• Same for longer absence (Pomponius D 41.2.25.2).

cards.front: Ulpianus (Labeo) D 41.2.6.1 (Case 52): B goes to market leaving nobody on his estate; A occupies it — does B lose possession?
cards.back:
Prevailing view (Ulpian): B loses possession only if he cannot evict A on his return.
• Labeo: A becomes possessor on entering; this view did not prevail.
• Temporary absence does not end CORPUS.

cards.front: What happens to possession of land when detentors or possessor's agents stop exercising control?
cards.back:
Usually retained SOLO ANIMO; lost immediately only if they are driven off by force.
• Death or leaving: retained until the possessor can re-establish CORPUS.
• Mental illness or sublease (chain of detentors): no effect.
• Forcible expulsion: drastic interruption, immediate loss (Papinianus D 41.2.44.2).

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about retaining or losing possession — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Has ANIMUS been given up, or all CORPUS lost?
• Movable (CUSTODIA) or immovable; special case SERVUS FUGITIVUS?
• Retention SOLO ANIMO: for how long; was CORPUS re-established?
• Intruder or detentor problem: attempt to regain, expulsion by force?
